source: the net shift of the population between districts was less than one individual per hundred residents in the 12 mo prior to each census.
evidence: This is an inference from the ANMR values calculated by the authors.

claim: The annual migration rate in Botswana was stable at ~10% for each year between 1981 and 2011.
source: The constancy of this value at each census suggests that the annual migration rate in Botswana was stable at ~10% for each year between 1981 and 2011.
evidence: This is an inference from the CMI values calculated at each census.

claim: Migration occurred within districts, as well as between districts, but migration between districts was more common.
source: We found that migration occurred within districts, as well as between districts, but that migration between districts was more common.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of census data.

claim: Even in 1981, at the beginning of the period of rapid urbanization, the migration network was highly connected.
source: Even in 1981, at the beginning of the period of rapid urbanization, the migration network was highly connected
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' network analysis.

claim: Large-scale population movements linked almost all of the districts in the country in 1981.
source: and therefore large-scale population movements linked almost all of the districts in the country.
evidence: This is an inference from the network connectivity analysis.

claim: At each census, although the number of urbanized districts increased (as did their population size), the vast majority of migratory flows between the rural and developing urban districts were balanced by counter-flows.
source: Notably, we found at each census, that although the number of urbanized districts increased (as did their population size) the vast majority of migratory flows between the rural and developing urban districts were balanced by counter-flows.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of migration networks.

claim: HIV could have diffused, via the migration networks, throughout Botswana.
source: Our results on migration networks show how a generalized epidemic had the potential to develop: HIV could have diffused, via the migration networks, throughout Botswana.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the migration network findings.

claim: HIV may have been circulating in Botswana in the 1970s, as HIV has an incubation period of 10–12 years.
source: this suggests that HIV may have been circulating in Botswana in the 1970s, as HIV has an incubation period of 10–12 y (Hendriks et al., 1993; Muñoz et al., 1989).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations about HIV incubation period.

claim: One phylogenetic study indicates that HIV was introduced into Botswana in the 1960s, but exponential growth did not begin until the 1980s.
source: One phylogenetic study indicates that HIV was introduced into Botswana in the 1960s, but exponential growth did not begin until the 1980s (Wilkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilkinson et al., 2015.

claim: HIV spread southward from Kinshasa via travelers on the railroad that was built in the 1800s.
source: Another study suggests that HIV spread southward from Kinshasa (the epicenter of the HIV epidemic) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo via travelers on the railroad that was built in the 1800s (Faria et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Faria et al., 2014.

claim: The railroad from Kinshasa goes through Francistown.
source: Notably, this railroad goes through Francistown, which is one of Botswana's two cities
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the railroad route.

claim: It is possible that HIV was introduced into the mining towns of Botswana from overseas or South Africa.
source: It is possible that HIV was introduced into the mining towns of Botswana from overseas or South Africa.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about HIV introduction routes.

claim: In the 1970s and 1980s, many young men from Botswana went to work in the mines in South Africa, returning as the mining industry became established in their home country.
source: In the 1970s and 1980s, many young men from Botswana went to work in the mines in South Africa, returning as the mining industry became established in their home country.
evidence: This is stated as historical knowledge about labor migration.

claim: By 1981, the migration networks (for women and men) linked almost every district in Botswana.
source: Our results show that, by 1981, the migration networks (for women and men) linked almost every district in Botswana.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' network analysis.

claim: HIV-infected migrants from Francistown and/or the mining towns could have seeded HIV sub-epidemics in multiple rural districts throughout the country.
source: This indicates that HIV-infected migrants from Francistown and/or the mining towns (where AIDS cases were first reported and HIV prevalence quickly rose to high levels) could have seeded HIV sub-epidemics in multiple rural districts throughout the country.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on migration network findings and HIV prevalence data.

claim: HIV could have spread widely within rural districts due to the high rates of within-district migration.
source: HIV could then have spread widely within these districts due to the high rates of within-district migration that we have found.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on within-district migration findings.

claim: Due to the high and continuous migration rates, the sub-epidemics in rural districts were likely to have been seeded numerous times by HIV-infected migrants.
source: Due to the high and continuous migration rates, the sub-epidemics in rural districts were likely to have been seeded numerous times by HIV-infected migrants.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on migration rate findings.

claim: When HIV was first introduced into rural districts, the sub-epidemics in these districts may have been maintained by source-sink dynamics.
source: When HIV was first introduced into rural districts, the sub-epidemics in these districts may have been maintained by source-sink dynamics (Okano et al., 2020)
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Okano et al., 2020.

claim: Migratory flows and counter-flows between high and low prevalence areas would have functioned as 'transmission corridors'.
source: These flows would have functioned as 'transmission corridors' (Okano et al., 2021)
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Okano et al., 2021.

claim: The highly connected migration networks, with high migratory flows and counter-flows, could have contributed to the development of Botswana's generalized epidemic by distributing HIV throughout the country in the general population.
source: Taken together, our results show that the highly connected migration networks, with high migratory flows and counter-flows, could have contributed to the development of Botswana's generalized epidemic by distributing HIV throughout the country in the general population.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the migration network findings.

claim: Migrants have been shown to be at high risk of acquiring HIV infection.
source: Migrants have been shown to be at high risk of acquiring HIV infection (Camlin and Charlebois, 2019; Dobra et al., 2017; Olawore et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Camlin and Charlebois, 2019; Dobra et al., 2017; Olawore et al., 2018.

claim: Due to migration alone, each year ~10% of the population of Botswana was at high risk of HIV infection.
source: our results suggest that, due to migration alone, each year ~10% of the population of Botswana was at high risk.
evidence: This is an inference from the migration rate findings and knowledge about migrant HIV risk.

claim: The migrants in Botswana were young women and men, a group generally at the highest risk of HIV infection through sexual transmission.
source: The migrants in Botswana were young women and men, a group generally at the highest risk of HIV infection through sexual transmission.
evidence: This is an inference from the age profile findings and knowledge about HIV risk.

claim: Mining towns and cities would have been transmission hot-spots due to high levels of risky sexual behavior and a high probability of encountering an HIV-infected individual as a sex partner.
source: Mining towns and cities would have been transmission hot-spots (for both women and men) due to high levels of risky sexual behavior (as evidenced by high HIV prevalence; Barnett et al., 2002; UNAIDS and World Health Organization, 2004) and a high probability of encountering an HIV-infected individual as a sex partner.
evidence: This is an inference based on HIV prevalence data and knowledge about transmission dynamics.

claim: Due to the high prevalence of HIV, high turnover rates, and a high level of connectivity to other districts, the mining towns and cities could have functioned as geographically defined core groups for sexual transmission.
source: Due to the high prevalence of HIV, high turnover rates, and a high level of connectivity to other districts, the mining towns and cities could have functioned as geographically defined core groups for sexual transmission (for both women and men).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on multiple findings.

claim: FSWs in Botswana can have an extremely high number of sex partners in mining towns and urban areas (~7 per week) and remain as FSWs for ~4 years.
source: For example, FSWs in Botswana can have an extremely high number of sex partners in mining towns and urban areas (~7 per week) and remain as FSWs for ~4 y (Ministry of Health Botswana, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ministry of Health Botswana, 2013.

claim: The mining towns and cities were both migration in-flow hubs and migration out-flow hubs.
source: Notably we found that the mining towns and cities were both migration in-flow hubs and migration out-flow hubs.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Rural-to-urban migration coupled with urban-to-rural migration could have been a very important driver in the Botswana epidemic becoming hyperendemic.
source: Therefore, rural-to-urban migration coupled with urban-to-rural migration could have been a very important driver in the Botswana epidemic becoming hyperendemic.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the migration hub findings.

claim: Migration, by changing an individual's sexual network and social environment, has been shown to increase the risk of acquiring HIV for both women and men.
source: This type of migration, by changing an individual's sexual network and social environment, has been shown to increase the risk of acquiring HIV for both women and men (Anglewicz et al., 2018; Camlin and Charlebois, 2019; Dzomba et al., 2019; Low et al., 2021; Olawore et al., 2018; Thorp et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Circular migrants have been shown to both have an increased risk of acquiring HIV, and of transmitting HIV.
source: Circular migrants have been shown to both have an increased risk of acquiring HIV, and of transmitting HIV (Camlin and Charlebois, 2019; Palk and Blower, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Camlin and Charlebois, 2019; Palk and Blower, 2015.

claim: The greater the number of trips and/or the duration of the trip, the greater the risk of HIV acquisition or transmission.
source: The greater the number of trips and/or the duration of the trip, the greater the risk (Palk and Blower, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Palk and Blower, 2015.

claim: The relative importance of migration and short-term mobility is likely to evolve over time as a generalized HIV epidemic diffuses through the population.
source: We note that both migration and short-term mobility are important, and their relative importance to each other is likely to evolve over time as a generalized HIV epidemic diffuses through the population.
evidence: This is speculation based on knowledge about HIV transmission dynamics.

claim: The relative importance of migration and short-term mobility is likely to vary amongst countries in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Their relative importance is also likely to vary amongst countries in sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: This is speculation based on knowledge about regional variation.

claim: Ravenstein analyzed the 1871 and 1881 censuses of Great Britain and Ireland, and calculated the flows of lifetime migrants to urban centers.
source: The urbanization process was first studied quantitatively by Ravenstein, who analyzed the 1871 and 1881 censuses of Great Britain and Ireland, and calculated the flows of lifetime migrants to urban centers (Ravenstein, 1885).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ravenstein, 1885.

claim: Ravenstein showed that internal migration from rural areas was essential to the growth of industrial cities and towns.
source: He showed that internal migration from rural areas was essential to the growth of industrial cities and towns.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ravenstein, 1885.

claim: Ravenstein demonstrated that migration was extremely important in changing settlement patterns and geographically redistributing the population in both Great Britain and Ireland.
source: Additionally, he demonstrated that migration was extremely important in changing settlement patterns and geographically redistributing the population in both Great Britain and Ireland.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ravenstein, 1885.

claim: At each census, generally the majority of rural-to-urban migratory flows were balanced by counter-flows from urban areas to rural villages.
source: In contrast, we found at each census, that generally the majority of rural-to-urban migratory flows were balanced by counter-flows from urban areas to rural villages.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of migration networks.

claim: Even though there was a very high migration rate, migration did not drive urbanization in Botswana.
source: Consequently, even though there was a very high migration rate, we found that migration did not drive urbanization
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' analysis of migration and urbanization.

claim: Migration had relatively little impact on geographically redistributing Botswana's population.
source: and also had relatively little impact on geographically redistributing Botswana's population.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' analysis using MEI and ANMR.

claim: Differences between Botswana and high-income countries, in the role of internal migration on urbanization, were due to in situ urbanization occurring in Botswana and high rural-to-urban migratory flows being balanced by high urban-to-rural counter-flows.
source: Differences between Botswana and high-income countries, in the role of internal migration on urbanization, were due to in situ urbanization occurring in Botswana (rather than the rapid growth of cities and towns as in high-income countries) and high rural-to-urban migratory flows being balanced by high urban-to-rural counter-flows.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of Botswana's urbanization with high-income countries.

claim: During the 30-year time period analyzed (1981–2011), population growth in Botswana was high: the population doubled.
source: During the 30-year time period that we have analyzed (1981–2011), population growth in Botswana was high: the population doubled.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of census data.

claim: Since 1990, in situ urbanization and high population growth rates have driven Africa's rapid growth in urbanization.
source: Notably, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development recently reported that since 1990, in situ urbanization and high population growth rates have driven Africa's rapid growth in urbanization (Moriconi-Ebrard et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moriconi-Ebrard et al., 2020.

claim: Africa has high migration rates and is one of the least urbanized places in the world.
source: Africa has high migration rates and is one of the least urbanized places in the world (United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, & Population Division, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, & Population Division, 2019.

claim: The number of urban residents in Africa approximately doubled between 1995 and 2015, and is projected to double again by 2040.
source: the number of urban residents on the continent approximately doubled between 1995 and 2015, and is projected to double again by 2040 (Lall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lall et al., 2017.

claim: The mathematical models currently being used to predict migratory flows in Africa have been developed based on migratory processes observed in high-income countries.
source: The mathematical models currently being used to predict migratory flows in Africa (Ciavarella and Ferguson, 2021; Marshall et al., 2018; Meredith et al., 2021) have been developed based on migratory processes that have been observed, and census data that have been collected, in high-income countries.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ciavarella and Ferguson, 2021; Marshall et al., 2018; Meredith et al., 2021.

claim: The gravity model and the radiation model make the central assumption that individuals are attracted to move to a new location based on the population size at the destination relative to the size at the origin, moving from the smaller to the larger population.
source: The two most commonly used predictive models, the gravity model (Stewart, 1948) and the radiation model (Simini et al., 2012), make the central assumption that individuals are attracted to move to a new location based on the population size at the destination relative to the size at the origin, moving from the smaller to the larger population.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stewart, 1948 and Simini et al., 2012.

claim: New mathematical models are needed to predict migration in Botswana, and potentially in other rapidly urbanizing countries in Africa where in situ urbanization is occurring.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that new mathematical models are needed to predict migration in Botswana, and – potentially – in other rapidly urbanizing countries in Africa where in situ urbanization is occurring.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that existing models' assumptions don't match Botswana's migration patterns.

claim: For the three-decade time period investigated, the number of international migrants to Botswana was much smaller than the number of internal migrants.
source: However, for the three-decade time period that we have investigated, the number of international migrants to Botswana was much smaller than the number of internal migrants (Statistics Botswana, 2014; Statistics Botswana, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Statistics Botswana, 2014; Statistics Botswana, 2015.

claim: The IPUMS-International data used are samples rather than the complete censuses.
source: Third, a potential limitation is that the IPUMS-International (Integrated Public Use Microdata Series-International) data that we used are samples rather than the complete censuses
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study methodology.

claim: It is generally not possible to obtain complete census data due to privacy reasons.
source: we used this approach as it is generally not possible to obtain complete census data due to privacy reasons.
evidence: This is stated as justification for using sample data.

claim: Botswana has recently achieved the 95-95-95 targets that UNAIDS specified needed to be reached by 2030 in order to eliminate HIV.
source: Botswana has recently achieved the 95-95-95 targets (Mine et al., 2022) that UNAIDS specified needed to be reached by 2030 in order to eliminate HIV
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mine et al., 2022.

claim: 95% of people living with HIV need to be diagnosed, 95% of the diagnosed need to be on treatment, and 95% of those on treatment need to be virally suppressed to eliminate HIV.
source: 95% of people living with HIV need to be diagnosed, 95% of the diagnosed need to be on treatment, and 95% of those on treatment need to be virally suppressed.
evidence: This is stated as the UNAIDS definition of the 95-95-95 targets.

claim: HIV transmission is continuing in Botswana.
source: However, transmission is continuing (Magosi et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Magosi et al., 2022.

claim: Urbanization and large-scale population movements are continuing in Botswana.
source: as is urbanization and large-scale population movements (Okano et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Okano et al., 2021.

claim: The same processes that contributed to the development of the generalized hyperendemic HIV epidemic in Botswana may prevent the elimination of HIV.
source: The same processes that we have identified that may have contributed to the development of the generalized hyperendemic HIV epidemic in Botswana may prevent the elimination of HIV.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings about migration and HIV transmission.

claim: All HIV epidemics in SSA are generalized.
source: All HIV epidemics in SSA are generalized
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HIV epidemics in sub-Saharan Africa.

claim: HIV can only diffuse through a population by the movement of people.
source: HIV can only diffuse through a population by the movement of people.
evidence: This is stated as a logical fact about HIV transmission.

claim: This study is the first to study population-level mobility patterns and rates in any country in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to study population-level mobility patterns and rates in any country in sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Migration networks in other countries with generalized HIV epidemics may be very different from Botswana's.
source: Migration networks in other countries with generalized HIV epidemics may be very different.
evidence: This is speculation about the generalizability of the findings.
